title: Vesak, the third time
hook: a third Vesak: what has changed in you since the first

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the history: a tradition broken from outside and within, and healed again and again. Your line: broken and healed. Whom did you thank? Today, the festival year begins. Day one thousand fifty-three.

A small clay lamp, a wick, a little oil. That's all it takes. On Vesak night, in Sri Lanka and other Theravada lands, lamps like that line windowsills and temple walls, and paper lanterns hang over the streets. You've been here twice before on this path. In your first year, Vesak arrived as a new word. In your second, you went deeper into Colombo's lanterns and the eight precepts. Now a third Vesak comes round, and a third lamp. Same moon. Same story. The question today is about the one holding the lamp.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP, A WICK, A LITTLE OIL.` → `THE SAME MOON, A THIRD TIME.` → `WHO HOLDS THE LAMP?`

segments.voice: First, the day itself, briefly. In Theravada lands, Vesak remembers the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away, all on the full moon of the month of Vesakha. People visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food, and light lamps. Second, why lamps. This path heard the line once already, when the stretch on teachers closed. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, near the end of his life, the Buddha tells Ananda not to look for some outside refuge. In Rhys Davids's translation: "Therefore, O Ânanda, be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves." A lamp on Vesak night honors the Buddha, and it also points back at the one who lights it. Third, a quiet surprise in that line. The Pali word behind lamp is dipa, and dipa can also mean island. Some translators write be lamps unto yourselves; others write be islands unto yourselves. Both pictures work. A lamp gives light in the dark. An island stands firm in a flood, like the island from yesterday's Dhammapada line. Fourth, the third time. A festival that comes back each year works a little like a mirror on a wall you pass. The mirror doesn't change. The one passing it may. Three Vesaks on this path is not a test, and there's no right answer to what it shows. Some people notice they know more. Some notice they need less. Some notice nothing much, and that's honest too. The Dhammapada asks, in Müller's words: "Why do you not seek a light, ye who are surrounded by darkness?" Tonight's lamp is a small, plain answer.
screen: `BORN, AWAKE, GONE, ONE FULL MOON.` · `BE YE LAMPS UNTO YOURSELVES.` · `DIPA: A LAMP, OR AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `THE SAME MOON. YOU, A THIRD TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: light a lamp. If you have a candle or a small light, light it now, safely. If not, picture one. Sit, and watch the flame for a few breaths. Then, gently, ask: what's different since I first heard the word Vesak on this path? Don't hunt for a big answer. Let whatever comes, come. A habit. A question. A name. Nothing at all. Just keep the flame in view and let the breath be slow. The bell holds the time.
Vesak. The full moon when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, and light lamps, a little light for each of us to carry. Today's word.
Your line: the third lamp. Tonight, before you sleep, turn every light off but one, and sit with that one for a minute before you switch it off. Day one thousand fifty-three.

howItsDone: On Vesak, Buddhists in Theravada lands visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food and light lamps and lanterns to remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing.

notes: Rhys Davids's DN 16 2.33 ('be ye lamps unto yourselves. Be ye a refuge to yourselves.') and Müller's Dhammapada 146 are quoted from memory; please verify the exact wording and punctuation.
The dipa (Sanskrit dipa/dvipa) double meaning, lamp or island, is stated as 'can also mean'; scholars discuss which is meant. Confirm phrasing.
The hook refers to this path's year-one Vesak (day 145) and year-two 'Vesak, deeper' (day 682, Colombo lanterns and eight precepts).
The practice asks an open question and offers several possible answers including 'nothing much', to avoid telling the listener what changed in them.

Editor pass: 'in many Buddhist lands' (hook, howItsDone) narrowed to Theravada lands (claims rule); the mirror image no longer tells the listener 'you do' change; the fork no longer says Ananda was 'afraid' (DN 16 2.32 has him hoping the Buddha will leave instructions about the order).

Audit pass: 'be ye lamps unto yourselves' was quoted on day 1030 (the teachers, closed) as well; the teach now names the callback, and its new angle (dipa, lamp or island) stands. Match pair 'doesn't change: you do' told the listener they had changed, against the editor's own fix in the teach; now 'the one passing may'. Rhys Davids DN 16 II.33 and Müller Dhp 146 checked: sound.
